title: Wall Street grills Bank of America over money laundering fine
detail:
Wall Street grills Bank of America over money laundering fine
AFP
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 2:36 PM CDT 2 min read
BAC
Trade BAC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan said the $1.2 billion fine resolves charges the bank violated US anti-money laundering laws (Fabrice COFFRINI)

Shares of Bank of America tumbled Wednesday as the lender faced pointed questions from Wall Street analysts over a $1.2 billion regulatory settlement that led to a big earnings miss.

US authorities announced the penalty late Tuesday afternoon, charging that the bank failed to properly report more than $5 billion in "suspicious transactions," some related to national security risks.

Bank of America on Wednesday reported third-quarter profits of $6.5 billion, down 17 percent from the year-ago period. That translated into 91 cents per share, compared with expectations for $1.10 per share.

Near 1830 GMT, shares of the giant US lender were down around six percent after earlier falling nearly nine percent, a reaction that reflects investor surprise at the announcement.

During Wednesday's earnings conference call, BofA executives were asked "how it gets to this point" and whether there was a misunderstanding of the rules.

"At the end of the day, I think we have agreed to call this a settlement and move forward, and so we are doing it," said Chief Executive Brian Moynihan.

"We understand what they need us to do," he said. "We're deep in the process of remediating."

The settlement follows a December 2024 cease-and-desist order from US regulators that hit BofA for "unsafe or unsound practices," including failure to timely file suspicious activity reports.

Moynihan said the bank has made progress in efforts to pass regulatory muster since the 2024 order, adding thousands of employees to work on compliance with bank secrecy laws.

Later in the call, Moynihan was asked to address "reputational confidence" after BofA's earlier assurances suggested the financial hit would not be significant.

"We're very confident that we're on the course," the CEO said. "The key was to get agreement to what the resolution was, and that we have"

Moynihan said the company had redeployed some staff to fulfill compliance obligations, meaning it won't mean additional costs in the future for these functions.

"We are repositioning people from other units as we get the efficiencies to this and then that will let the head count drain down," he said.

title: Bank of America just drew a line in the sand for the stock market
detail:
Bank of America just drew a line in the sand for the stock market
Hillary Remy, Celine Provini
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 1:47 PM CDT 6 min read
BAC
Trade BAC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Professional investors have been telling each other for months that rising Treasury yields are the main threat to the equity rally.

Bank of America's October survey put a specific number on when that threat becomes a real problem.

The October Global Fund Manager Survey, which polled more than 300 investment professionals, found that the 10-year Treasury yield would need to reach 5.9% before managers shift meaningfully out of stocks and into bonds, CNBC reported.

The survey described that level as "nearly 6%." With the 10-year yield tracking around 4.64% heading into the fourth quarter, the gap between current levels and that threshold is more than a full percentage point.

That distance is doing a lot of work in how institutional money is positioned right now, and the survey captures both where managers are willing to sit and what they are actually worried about.

Also read: Michael Burry doubles down on his stock market stand

The Treasury yield number that would force a real rotation out of stocks

Treasury yields and stock valuations pull against each other in a direct way. As yields rise, the discount rate applied to future corporate earnings goes up. That makes those earnings worth less in today's terms and puts pressure on stock prices.

The question portfolio managers are always working through is the yield level at which bonds begin to look more attractive than equities. For the managers in BofA's survey, that level is 5.9%.

Getting from 4.64% to 5.9% would require one of the larger yield surges in recent memory. That kind of move does not typically happen without a visible catalyst, whether that is an inflation surprise, a significant fiscal shock, or a breakdown in demand at Treasury auctions.

Survey respondents are clearly not expecting any of those things soon, which is the underlying reason they are comfortable staying long equities at current levels.

The survey also found that 76% of managers expect the Federal Reserve to hold rates steady at its October meeting.

A Fed on hold reduces the likelihood of near-term upward pressure on yields from the policy side. That expectation is reinforcing the sense among managers that 5.9% remains a distant scenario heading into year-end.

For investors watching yields and trying to understand when that movement starts to hurt stock returns, the survey provides a concrete reference point.Bloomberg / Getty Images
Where institutional money is concentrating risk right now

Technology allocations in the survey reached their highest point since August 2020. That reading covers roughly six years of fund manager surveys, and the driver behind it is not hard to identify: The artificial intelligence buildout has pulled institutional capital into tech at a pace that has steadily reset the upper end of what normal positioning looks like.

title: Why Did No One at Bank of America Go to Prison Like CZ??
detail:
Why Did No One at Bank of America Go to Prison Like CZ??
Lockridge Okoth
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 1:09 PM CDT 3 min read
BAC
Trade BAC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Bank of America stock fell as much as 9% on Wednesday, a day after the bank admitted willful money laundering control failures and agreed to pay $1.21 billion. Nobody was charged with a crime.

Changpeng Zhao (CZ) served four months in a US prison over his exchange's anti-money laundering (AML) failures. On Wednesday, the Binance executive highlighted this double standard.

What Bank of America Admitted and Why Shares Fell

According to the Treasury, the bank failed to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions on time. Over $1 billion involved national security risks, including suspected Chinese money laundering networks.

The release says the bank often relied on law enforcement inquiries to spot problems, rather than its own monitoring.

The penalty cut quarterly profit by 17 cents a share, as BeInCrypto flagged Tuesday. Even without it, adjusted earnings of $1.08 per share missed estimates, per TipRanks.

Meanwhile, CZ referred to deferred prosecution agreements (DPAs), deals where prosecutors drop charges if a company complies.

Why Did No One at Bank of America Face Charges?

The penalties came from three Treasury agencies. These are civil regulators, and they issue fines, not criminal charges.

Criminal cases come from the Justice Department. None of Tuesday's Treasury announcements mention it.

That department changed course in 2025. A May 2025 Criminal Division memo widened the paths for companies to avoid prosecution if they self-report, cooperate, and fix problems.

Law firm Paul Weiss counted 21 corporate guilty pleas in 2025 and read the data as a slowdown. In 2013, then-Attorney General Eric Holder told senators that the size of some banks made them difficult to prosecute.

Why an HSBC Whistleblower Wants Bank of America Executives Charged

Everett Stern reported money laundering at HSBC while working there as a compliance officer in 2010. On Wednesday, he published an open letter on X to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Stern asked Bessent to refer Bank of America executives for criminal prosecution. He also urged an end to "too big to jail" and a review of the bank's national charter.

HSBC settled its own case in December 2012. It admitted that at least $881 million in cartel drug money moved through its US arm, according to the Justice Department.

HSBC paid about $1.92 billion and signed a deferred prosecution agreement. Stern says no banker was charged, and that reporting the bank cost him his career.

"The fines are not working. A fine is paid by shareholders, absorbed by the balance sheet, and forgotten by the next earnings call."

(Updates with latest market prices and developments.)

US benchmark equity indexes declined intraday as markets assessed a hot inflation report and an earnings miss at Bank of America (BAC).

The Nasdaq Composite was down 1.7% at 26,750.6 after midday Wednesday and the S&P 500 fell 1.1% to 7,720.4. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 0.3% to 51,508.6.

Among sectors, technology led the laggards, while healthcare paced the gainers.

In economic news, US consumer inflation accelerated in September as gasoline prices surged, while the core measure unexpectedly remained steady, official data showed. The report increased the odds for an interest rate increase in October.

"With core inflation running at 2.6% year-on-year and oil prices remaining elevated, which increases the risk that price pressures spread to other categories, the Fed likely will not be able to remain on the sidelines for much longer," TD Economics said in a note.

The probability of the US central bank hiking rates by 25 basis points on Oct. 28 rose to 35% on Wednesday from 22% on Tuesday, according to the CME FedWatch tool. Markets are pricing in a 63% probability that the benchmark rate will be kept steady, down from 78%.

Treasury yields were higher intraday, with the two-year rate up 5.3 basis points at 4.85%, and the 10-year rate was up 2.1 basis points to 5.24%.

Bank of America's third-quarter results missed market expectations due to a regulatory settlement charge and weak trading and investment banking revenue. Morgan Stanley (MS) topped estimates on an equity trading revenue boost.

Shares of Bank of America were down 5.3% intraday, while Morgan Stanley fell 3.2%.

BlackRock (BLK) reported an unexpected increase in third-quarter net inflows driven by strong institutional demand and retail inflows. Shares of the company were up 0.2%.

Dell (DELL) shares tumbled 11%, the second-worst performer on the S&P 500, while Nvidia (NVDA) dropped 2.7%, the Dow's second-biggest decliner. Honeywell (HON) unveiled an industrial AI simulation platform built with Nvidia and Dell. Honeywell shares were up 0.6%.

West Texas Intermediate crude oil gained 1.4% to $95.48 a barrel, while Brent rose 0.7% to $106.42.

Spot gold fell 2% to $4,079.19 per troy ounce, while silver slumped 6.4% to $55.71 per ounce.
